{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nc-c","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"57a869466f9db7623a402d19cc8355b0dc53df15934c8e6bf5d2f4002d05abdb","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nc-class-c:lineage:64","source_registry_sha256":"e128656a3d00ba5437556728ebd87f5842c83601163739613417fe77cf9f423b","source_liveness_sha256":"dbfdf3e6d892a41c42c05809a9213d44a78aedd480dc6de23937c97292428b74"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Traffic signs and pavement markings","heading":"C — Regulatory, warning and guide signs by shape and color, route markers, pavement lines and markers, and traffic officer signals (North Carolina)","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Regulatory, warning and guide signs by shape and color, route markers, pavement lines and markers, and traffic officer signals (North Carolina)
Knowledge domain: the three types of North Carolina traffic signs and how shape and color identify them, highway route markers and numbering, the meaning of yellow and white pavement lines and colored reflective markers, and how to obey a traffic officer's signals.

FACT_ID: sec15-F01 | anchor: A01
Shape and color let you identify the kind of highway sign at a glance, and signs fall into three types: regulatory, warning and guide or informational. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec15-F02 | anchor: A01
The eight-sided octagon is used only for stop signs, which show white STOP lettering on a red background. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec15-F03 | anchor: A01
A stop sign is usually placed 6 to 50 feet before the intersection, and the law requires a full stop there. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec15-F04 | anchor: A01
After stopping at a stop sign, do not move again until you are certain the way is clear. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec15-F05 | anchor: A01
When a sign or signal requires a stop, stop at the marked stop line; with no stop line or crosswalk, stop before entering the intersection at a point where you can see the cross street. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec15-F06 | anchor: A01
The yield sign is a red and white triangle pointing down, and it requires you to slow down and give the right of way. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec15-F07 | anchor: A01
At a yield sign, whether you must stop depends on cross traffic; if needed to avoid interfering with it, stop and wait until it passes. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec15-F08 | anchor: A01
Rectangular and square regulatory signs, usually black and white or red and white, show speed limits and rules such as NO U-TURN, and disobeying them is a traffic violation. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec15-F09 | anchor: A01
A handicap parking sign reserves the space for qualifying people who display a handicap license plate or dashboard placard. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec15-F10 | anchor: A02
The yellow pennant-shaped sign sits on the left side of the road and marks the start of a no-passing zone, reinforcing the rectangular DO NOT PASS sign. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec15-F11 | anchor: A02
Diamond-shaped signs give cautions or warnings and are normally black on yellow. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec15-F12 | anchor: A02
A diamond sign in black on orange warns of a construction or maintenance area, so drive with extra care. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec15-F13 | anchor: A02
The STOP AHEAD warning sign is placed well before a stop sign whose view is blocked by a curve or other objects. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec15-F14 | anchor: A02
A round yellow sign with a black X and the letters RR warns of a railroad crossing ahead, so slow down and stop if needed to cross safely. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec15-F15 | anchor: A02
The crossbuck at the tracks reads RAILROAD CROSSING in black on white crosspieces. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec15-F16 | anchor: A02
Once stopped for a train signal, gate or flagger, stay stopped until the gate rises or the signal or flagger shows it is safe. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec15-F17 | anchor: A02
Before crossing railroad tracks, look twice in each direction. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec15-F18 | anchor: A03
The five-sided pentagon sign warns of a school zone or school crossing, where you should watch especially for children. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec15-F19 | anchor: A03
In many school zones the speed limit is lowered during certain school hours. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec15-F20 | anchor: A03
Guide and informational signs give directions, routes, distances and the locations of services. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec15-F21 | anchor: A03
Odd-numbered highways generally run north and south, and even-numbered highways generally run east and west. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec15-F22 | anchor: A03
U.S. highway route markers are shield shaped, while North Carolina route markers are diamond shaped. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec15-F23 | anchor: A03
North Carolina secondary road signs are rectangular, and interstate highways use a red, white and blue shield. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec15-F24 | anchor: A03
Blue and white signs point to a nearby hospital, Highway Patrol station or telephone. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec15-F25 | anchor: A03
Rectangular guide signs may be green, brown or blue and give directions and distances. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec15-F26 | anchor: A03
Never stop in the middle of the road to read a sign; when safe, pull onto the shoulder and work out your route there. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec15-F27 | anchor: A04
The DO NOT STOP ON TRACKS sign reminds drivers never to stop on a railroad track for any reason. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec15-F28 | anchor: A05
Yellow lines divide lanes going in opposite directions, and white lines divide lanes going the same direction. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec15-F29 | anchor: A05
A broken yellow center line on a two-lane, two-way road means careful passing is allowed in both directions. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec15-F30 | anchor: A05
Double solid yellow center lines may not be crossed to pass from either direction. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec15-F31 | anchor: A05
On a two-lane road you may pass with care when the broken yellow line is on your side. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec15-F32 | anchor: A05
A single solid white line marks the right edge of the road, and a single solid yellow line marks the left edge on a divided highway. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec15-F33 | anchor: A05
If the white edge line is on your left and the yellow edge line on your right, you are going the wrong way. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec15-F34 | anchor: A05
A center two-way left-turn lane on some multi-lane highways is only for left turns from either direction, never for passing or merging. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec15-F35 | anchor: A05
White and yellow reflective pavement markers make lane lines easier to see on wet roads at night, while red markers warn that you are going the wrong way. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec15-F36 | anchor: A05
In some areas, blue reflective markers in the road show where fire hydrants or water supplies are for firefighters. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec15-F37 | anchor: A05
When a traffic officer is directing traffic, obey the officer's hand signals instead of the usual signals or signs. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec15-F38 | anchor: A05
An officer usually signals stop with a raised palm facing the vehicle and a long whistle blast, and signals go with a hand motion and a series of short blasts. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec15-F39 | anchor: A05
At night, a traffic officer may give signals with a flashlight. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0090]

Misconceptions: the octagon is never used for anything but a stop sign; a yield sign does not always require a stop, only when cross traffic demands it; black on orange means a work area, not an ordinary warning; a broken yellow line on the other side does not let you pass; the two-way left-turn lane is not a passing lane; an officer's signal overrides a green light.
Mnemonics: eight sides stop, three sides yield, five sides school; yellow divides opposing traffic, white divides same-direction traffic; odd goes north and south, even goes east and west; red markers mean wrong way.
Glossary: regulatory sign means a sign stating a rule you must obey; warning sign means a sign alerting you to a hazard ahead; guide sign means a sign giving routes, distances or services; pennant means the long triangular yellow no-passing sign on the left; two-way left-turn lane means a shared center lane for left turns in both directions.
Dynamic facts: school zone speed reductions and their hours are set locally and are posted on site, so none are stated here.
